analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate tobacco products, restrict youth-targeted marketing, and require stronger warnings.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate health committee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made tobacco products subject to Food and Drug Administration oversight, treating them like other products the agency regulates. Makers would have had to disclose ingredients and nicotine content, submit health research to the government, meet manufacturing and performance standards, and put stronger warnings on packages and ads. It would also let states restrict cigarette advertising again, something a 1992 federal law had blocked, and it would apply the same rules to tobacco shipped overseas. The bill was introduced after the Supreme Court ruled that the FDA had no power over tobacco without new legislation, and it died in committee without a single hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Young people, who the bill's findings say make up nearly all new tobacco users and are especially influenced by advertising. Adults who smoke would get clearer warnings and disclosure of ingredients and nicotine delivery. State and local governments would regain the power to restrict tobacco advertising and promotion, and taxpayers would bear less of the medical cost of smoking-related disease.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young people and state health regulators

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services, through the FDA, authority to regulate the manufacture, marketing, and distribution of tobacco products as the primary federal regulator.

Manufacturers would have to disclose every ingredient by brand and quantity, report nicotine content and delivery, and hand over all internal research on health and dependency effects of their products.
The FDA could set performance standards, including reducing or eliminating nicotine yields and other harmful constituents, and could require premarket review of new tobacco products.
It revises warning requirements for cigarettes and smokeless tobacco and removes the provision that blocks states from imposing their own advertising or promotion restrictions.
The bill's own findings estimate that cutting youth smoking by half would prevent more than 60,000 early deaths each year and save up to $43 billion annually in medical costs and lost productivity.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would bear the cost of registration, ingredient disclosure, inspections, premarket applications, and advertising limits. Tobacco growers would be shielded: the bill explicitly exempts tobacco leaf, growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives from FDA authority. Adult smokers could face fewer product choices and higher compliance costs passed through prices, and companies would lose the marketing tools the bill says are aimed at young people.

drawbacks.text: Restrictions on advertising and the power to cap nicotine raise commercial-speech and adult-choice concerns: the bill would leave cigarettes legal for adults while limiting how they can be marketed and how the product can be made.

The regulatory machine would be costly to build and run: registration, biennial factory inspections, advisory committee reviews, and 180-day premarket review deadlines all add federal bureaucracy, and compliance burdens on manufacturers are explicitly acknowledged in the bill's own reporting requirements.
The bill carves tobacco farming entirely out of FDA authority, so the upstream supply chain that feeds manufacturers would remain untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside, per the bill's own findings, is enormous: tens of thousands of early deaths prevented each year if youth smoking drops. The costs fall on a small, highly profitable industry and flow partly into prices paid by adult users, who would keep legal access to cigarettes. The main design weakness is the farm carve-out, which limits how far the regulation reaches. On balance the benefits to public health clearly outweigh the compliance costs, and an honest supporter would concede the advertising limits constrain adult-facing commercial speech.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on May 16, 2000, with introductory remarks recorded in the Congressional Record.
Four Democratic senators — Frank Lautenberg, Dick Durbin, John Kerry, and Paul Wellstone — signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans did.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction.
The action history shows no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill would have given the FDA broad authority over tobacco products, mandated stronger warnings, restored state advertising authority, and imposed export requirements on tobacco products.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: the bill died without a vote, so the industry continued operating without federal product regulation. Congress did not give the FDA tobacco authority until 2009, nine years later. The committee's inaction also spared tobacco advertisers and retailers the marketing restrictions the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Jim Jeffords
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Tobacco manufacturers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against federal tobacco regulation during this period; the industry spent close to $4.9 billion in 1995 on marketing to attract and retain users, per the bill's own findings, and fought FDA oversight in court and in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the record shows no party split; all five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill's fate was decided by committee inaction, not a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would subject cigarette and smokeless tobacco makers to FDA registration, inspections, ingredient and nicotine disclosure, performance standards, and premarket review, and would end the marketing practices the bill says target young users. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the public-health goal of reducing youth smoking.

The bill deems violating advertisements deceptive, mandates text-heavy warnings on ads, and restores state power to restrict tobacco promotion. Media and sports organizations that sold tobacco sponsorships would lose that revenue stream.

The bill explicitly exempts tobacco leaf, growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives from FDA authority and bars inspectors from entering farms without written consent, locking the agricultural side of the industry out of regulation entirely. This carve-out protected growers from any compliance cost while the bill regulated manufacturers downstream.
